title: Your Phone's GPS Needs EINSTEIN 🛰️
description:
Your phone's GPS needs Einstein. Up in space, time runs faster: gravity slows clocks down, so your clock down here drags, and the clocks on GPS satellites gain about 38 millionths of a second every day. Sounds tiny? To GPS, that's over 10 kilometres of error, a day. The first test satellite even flew with the fix switched off, in case Einstein was wrong. He wasn't.
Did you know your phone uses relativity? Yes or no?

The science: GPS satellites orbit about 20,000 km up at about 14,000 km/h. Their speed makes their atomic clocks tick slower than ours by about 7 microseconds a day (special relativity), but the weaker gravity up there makes them tick faster by about 45 microseconds a day (general relativity), so they run about 38 microseconds a day fast. GPS finds you by timing radio signals that cross about 30 cm in a billionth of a second, so 38 microseconds is about 11 km: uncorrected, the errors would build up by more than 10 km in a single day (Neil Ashby, Physics Today, 2002; Richard Pogge, Ohio State University). That is why every GPS clock is set to tick slightly slow before launch. When the first test satellite, NTS-2, was launched in 1977, the size of the effect, and even its sign, was uncertain, and some doubted it was real, so its correction was built in switched off. After about 20 days of measuring, the clock ran fast just as relativity predicted, to within 1 %, and the correction was switched on.
